_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 4 Mathematics unit lecture film, Where Things Are. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. The chapters follow the lesson's own three parts (compass points, coordinates, turns and angles) and its own slides: the four cardinal points and a quarter turn (slide 1), the ordinal points and where their names come from (slide 2), a two-move route on the 8 by 8 map (slides 3 and 4), along first then up (slides 5 and 6), the corners of a rectangle (slide 7), and a mirror line on the shape's own edge (slides 8 and 9). Every number said is the lesson's: Hodan's 3 east then 2 north, the point (3, 2), the rectangle with corners (1, 1) and (4, 3).
title: Where Things Are
subtitle: Grade 4 Mathematics
objectives: Interpret and create descriptions of position, direction and movement, including reference to cardinal and ordinal points, and their notations.
Understand that position can be described using coordinate notation. Read and plot coordinates in the first quadrant (with the aid of a grid).
Reflect 2D shapes in a horizontal or vertical mirror line, including where the mirror line is the edge of the shape, on square grids.

beats.say: Where is it? And which way? A grid and a compass answer both.
Eight compass points, and a pair of numbers for every place.
A compass always has four main points on every map.
North, east, south and west, going round in that order.
You are facing north. Now make a quarter turn clockwise.
You are facing east. Each quarter turn moves you on one point.
A quarter turn is a right angle. Four turns make a full turn.
Between north and east there sits one more point.
Its name is both names joined together: north-east.
South and west join in the same way, to make south-west.
There are four of these in-between points, one in each gap.
That makes eight in all, and north or south always comes first.
A route is moves, one after another, in order.
Hodan starts on this square. North is up the grid.
She walks three squares east. Count them: one, two, three.
Then she walks two squares north, up two rows.
She is still three squares east of her start. North changed the row, not the column.
This grid has numbers along the bottom and up the side.
A coordinate is a pair of numbers, like three and two.
Go along three first, then go up two squares.
That lands on the point. Along first, then up, every time.
Swap them and you are somewhere else. Two along and three up is a different place.
A shape sits on the grid. Every corner has its own pair.

at.shape: A shape sits on the grid

beats.say: This corner here is one along and one up.
The corner opposite is four along and three up.
The other two borrow one number from each of those.
Read every corner the same way: along the bottom, then up the side.
A mirror line runs down the grid, along the edge of this shape.
Every square receives a partner, the same distance the other side.
This square is right against the line, so its partner touches it.
This is two squares back, so its partner is two squares out.
All six squares cross over, and the picture is twice as wide.
Eight compass points name every direction. A quarter turn is a right angle.
A route is moves in order. A coordinate is along first, then up.
Every corner has its own pair.
And a mirror gives every square its partner.
